tooltip.midicraft.mod_enabled: Master switch for everything the mod does out in the world: the labels over note blocks and repeaters, scrolling to retune them, and the placement sequence. The Composer is not affected and its key still opens it with this off.
tooltip.midicraft.debug_commands: Adds two subcommands: /midicraft paste builds a run of chords you type out rather than a song, and asciidiagram draws a region as text. They appear and disappear from tab-completion as this moves, and refuse to run while it is off. The README has the syntax.
tooltip.midicraft.radial_focus_delay: Ticks the center label must stay under the crosshair before its radial opens and accepts scrolling. 0 opens immediately.
tooltip.midicraft.repeater_control_style: Radial select shows a four-number diamond and lets either wheel direction confirm a hovered delay. Scroll uses one number with directional cycling.
tooltip.midicraft.invert_scroll: Makes wheel-down raise the selected pitch instead of wheel-up.
tooltip.midicraft.view_distance: Maximum distance at which note and repeater labels are shown.
tooltip.midicraft.interaction_delay: Extra ticks between tuning interactions. 0 restores the original maximum of one interaction per client tick.
tooltip.midicraft.wait_for_ack: Waits for the changed block state to return from the server before sending the next interaction. Safer on restrictive or laggy servers, but slower.
tooltip.midicraft.require_line_of_sight: Cancels tuning if another block obstructs the path from your eyes to the target block. Disabled by default.
tooltip.midicraft.sequence_enabled: Runs or pauses the placement sequence without resetting its position, which is remembered per song. Double-tap the sequence key to switch between running and paused.
tooltip.midicraft.sequencing_edit_protec: While a nonempty sequence is running, disables overlay editing and optionally blocks ordinary right-click changes to existing note blocks and repeaters. Sneak-placement and automatic tuning remain available.
tooltip.midicraft.select_harp_blocks: Whether harp notes stop for a block of their own when Select instruments is on. Off, a harp note is a single step and you place only the note block. On, it asks for grass or dirt like any other instrument.
tooltip.midicraft.chord_place_order: The order the sequencer walks the notes of one chord, which is built two notes to a block of bus. 2 strips walks the top row then comes back along the bottom, which is what a hand carrying one stack does. Alternating crosses the bus at every note. Neither moves a note.
tooltip.midicraft.select_instruments: Makes the block under a note a step of its own, since a note block takes its instrument from what it stands on. Each note waits for its instrument first: the tile lights up, the hotbar picks that block out, and a wrong block waits rather than counting.
tooltip.midicraft.auto_select_sequence_b: Selects a note block or repeater from your hotbar whenever the current sequence step changes, including manual scrolling.
tooltip.midicraft.max_build_floors: Upper limit on how many floors a Compact cube build may stack. The layout picks whichever count comes out closest to a cube, so raising this shrinks the footprint of a long song and keeps more of it within earshot. Each floor is four blocks tall.
tooltip.midicraft.commands_per_tick: How fast the Place tracks button sends its setblock commands. Higher finishes a build far sooner and is usually fine in singleplayer, but a server may treat a high rate as command spam and disconnect you. The three slowest settings send one command every two, three or four ticks, which is the pace a strict server will tolerate. A build reaching past your loaded chunks pauses at the edge either way, and resumes when you walk to it.
tooltip.midicraft.midi_quantize_grid: Grid that Edit > Convert for Minecraft snaps note starts onto, so the gaps between them become whole repeater delays. Auto reads a grid from the song’s own spacing. This is a conversion setting, not an import one: importing never quantizes anything.
tooltip.midicraft.midi_instrument_source: Where each imported track's note-block instrument comes from. The MIDI file reads its General MIDI program changes, so a bass track arrives as a bass and channel 10 arrives as drums. Track names adds a fallback for files that never send one: a track called "Lead Saw" becomes a bit, "Kick" becomes a bass drum. Always the default gives every track the instrument below, which is what imports did before this setting.
option.midicraft.convert_octave_shifting: Shift the layer, then the notes
tooltip.midicraft.convert_octave_shiftin: What Convert moves to bring a layer into the note-block range, and there are two ways to read the question. Two of them move the pitch. Shift the notes moves only the notes that are out of range, each by its own nearest octave, and leaves everything else exactly where it was written. Shift the layer moves the whole layer to wherever the fewest of its notes are out of range, then shifts whatever is still out note by note — fewer split layers, at the cost that notes with nothing wrong with them can move. The other two move the notes instead, onto a melodic split layer that plays F#1 to F#7 at true pitch, so an octave-wide bass line survives intact. Split into melodic sends the strays there, high and low to the same layer, and leaves the rest of the part on its own instrument — one layer added per part that straddles the range. Convert to melodic turns the whole part into that layer the moment one note needs it: no layer is added at all, which is what a song near the layer limit needs, but the part gives up its instrument and plays by register instead. All four end with every note in range, and always by whole octaves: a part moved by anything else is in a different key from the rest of the song. Mind the blocks on the melodic two — the tiers overlap by an octave and a split layer sounds every voice that covers a note, so anything in an overlap builds twice on two lanes until you drag a bracket in.
tooltip.midicraft.convert_split_transpos: When a note takes a different octave from the rest of its layer, give it a layer of its own, named with the octave it moved. Nothing about a layer requires this — it is so you can see what Convert moved, mute it, or put it back. Off keeps the layer whole and the layer count down, and two notes an octave apart that land on one pitch become one note instead of one dropped layer. A wide part still splits either way if no single octave holds it. Says nothing under either melodic mode: Split into melodic always makes exactly one companion per part, because a melodic layer is what it has to move the notes onto, and Convert to melodic makes none at all.
tooltip.midicraft.conversion_gap_percent: Share of the closest note gaps the automatic convert grid may ignore when choosing its resolution. Without this, a single pair of notes closer together than the rest sets the grid, and therefore the tempo, for the whole song. Ignored notes are quantized onto the grid and shift slightly. 0 uses the strict smallest gap.
tooltip.midicraft.repeat_merge_ticks: When converting for Minecraft, collapses a repeat of the same pitch that arrives within this many repeater ticks into the note before it. Songs that fake a sustain by re-triggering a note every tick are otherwise unbuildable, and force the whole song to be slowed down to fit them. 0 keeps every repeat.
tooltip.midicraft.midi_velocity_cutoff: Drops imported notes quieter than this MIDI velocity, on both MIDI and NBS import. Off by default, because a cutoff inside a file’s own range removes music rather than noise, and a fade-in loses its opening. Note blocks have no volume, so quiet notes still cost a block each — but that is a decision better made in the Composer, where you can see them.
tooltip.midicraft.chord_thin_target: How many note blocks a chord may hold. Over it, preview and the build lower counted instruments and skip sustain strikes, as the two settings below allow, and Select > Overloaded chords suggests notes to delete from whatever is still over. A build places 30 at one instant and no more. Thinning never drops the last of a pitch or the last of an instrument.
tooltip.midicraft.chord_thin_volume: On a chord over the target, play counted instruments with fewer copies: one at a time off whichever has the most, never below one. Runs before skipping strikes, because a copy less is the least a chord can lose. Nothing is deleted, and the full count plays wherever the chord has room.
tooltip.midicraft.chord_thin_strikes: On a chord still over the target, skip a sustain strike. The held note rings on from the strike before, and never loses two in a row. Nothing is deleted.
tooltip.midicraft.midi_ignore_percussion: Skips MIDI channel 10, which is usually drums.
tooltip.midicraft.midi_default_instrumen: Instrument id used for imported tracks, such as HARP, BASS, BELL, FLUTE, or MUTE.
error.midicraft.sequence: Notes must be 0-24 and repeater delay groups must be 1d-64d.
tooltip.midicraft.lane_one_block: What the first machine's plain lane is built from: the floor its wire and repeaters stand on. Needs a top that dust and repeaters can stand on, and nothing more, so glass or a slab will do. The cells that have to carry power take the relay block instead. Light show lamps and the block under each note, which is its instrument, are left alone. A color-coded paste keeps its colours.
tooltip.midicraft.lane_two_block: The same for the second machine, the one playing the other half of the game tick. Set it apart from lane one to see where each machine runs.
tooltip.midicraft.relay_block: What the lane is built from wherever it has to carry power, in both machines: the bus, stacked chords, the double rail and a descent's powered rungs, and anything standing over or beside dust to keep its steps from connecting where they should not. Has to conduct redstone. Stone by default.
tooltip.midicraft.transparent_block: What the climbs between floors are built from, glass by default. Dust runs up over it, so it must not conduct redstone and needs a top that dust can sit on. Glass under a note is that note's instrument and stays glass.
tooltip.midicraft.support_block: The level under a floor: what holds up falling instruments, dust and the bottom rail's repeaters. Needs a solid top. A slab is laid as its top half. Nothing here carries power.
tooltip.midicraft.nearby_overlays: Labels drawn over every block of these types within view distance, whether or not you are looking at one. Something to read, not to use — retuning a block is the interactive overlay below. Off leaves nearby blocks unlabelled.
tooltip.midicraft.interactive_overlays: The overlay on the block under your crosshair, which you can scroll to retune. This is what the overlay key turns on and off. It works whether or not nearby overlays are showing: with those off, you see and change the one block you are aiming at and nothing else.
tooltip.midicraft.interactive_overlay_ty: Which block types the interactive overlay answers for. Narrow it to repeaters if scrolling note blocks by accident is the problem, or the other way about.
tooltip.midicraft.all_keys: Vanilla’s own key bindings screen, where every mod’s keys are listed together. The three above are the same bindings, shown here so you do not have to go looking.
tooltip.midicraft.composer_gui_scale: GUI scale for this mod’s own screens, separate from Minecraft’s. A piano roll wants pixels, and the scale that suits a hotbar rarely shows four bars of a song at once. Same as Minecraft leaves the game’s scale alone; anything else applies while one of these screens is open and is put back when you close to the world. The window clamps whatever will not fit.
